item.title: Recent Outages Have Economic Causes
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie.Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits.Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful until something bad happens.But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement.But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

item.title: Formlabs Form Studio 1 Teardown
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: Formlabs has recently launched the Form Studio 1. I’ve had fun tearing down every new generation of their printers. I am pleased to continue that tradition, and to share the joy of learning by taking apart someone else’s product.Financial interest disclosure: Formlabs provided me with the printer for this teardown, with no contingencies on the contents or views expressed in this post. I am also a shareholder of Formlabs.The Form Studio 1 picks up where the Form 4 SLA printer leaves off. For details, you can review the teardown of the Form 4. The key point is that the Form 4 represented a watershed moment in Formlabs’ evolution from a galvanometer based printer to an LCD shutter based printer. The basic architecture of the Form 4, and the Form Studio 1, is reviewed in the diagram below.While the architecture of the Form Studio 1 mirrors that of the Form 4, the Form Studio 1 retails at roughly a quarter the price of a Form 4. This addresses one of the biggest pain points about the Formlabs printer line-up: the high base price of the printer. Since a big theme of the Form Studio 1 is cost reduction, let’s first explore some of the cost drivers in building products like printers.Complex electromechanical systems are expensive to assemble. The main driver is the cost of labor: a screw costs a fraction of a cent; the labor to install the screw is far larger. Furthermore, there is a big difference in the skills required between a person who only puts one screw into a single hole all day long, and someone who has to keep track of a fifty-step build, routing cables from a diverse number of endpoints, while attaching screws with the correct amount of torque and possibly other bespoke requirements such as thread lockers. A good production-line setup can go a long way to fool-proof the build process – e.g. pre-kitting parts, kanban systems, etc. – but these systems also cost money to set up and run, and the overhead only becomes negligible at the highest volumes.For complex, high-BOM cost builds, the cost of rework is also an important consideration. The high cost of materials means it’s almost never acceptable to simply scrap defective assemblies. However, complex builds have a low net yield, especially in the early phase of the production ramp. The statistics are daunting: a 50-step build where each step is 99% reliable would only yield 60% good product; at 100 steps, you’re well under 40% yield. Worse yet, the problem is often going to be a single subtle issue in just one step out of many, so you’re left looking for a needle in a haystack. This type of task requires the expertise of a senior technician, who bills at a higher rate.Thus, the most effective way to reduce cost is to simply design it out. One metric I can use to compare the Form Studio 1 to the Form 4 is how long it took to do the teardown. The Form 4 took me almost two solid weeks, on and off, of trying to figure out how all the parts came together. When I do a teardown, I try to envision the production flow and reverse it. The Form 4 had several forks in the process that I had to experiment with before I figured out a clean reverse flow. Even then, there were a couple assemblies whose build order I could not figure out. Eventually I gave up, and just tore them apart with brute force.In contrast, the bulk of the Form Studio 1 took me about two afternoons to tear down. The inverse flow was intuitive. At a minimum, this is a strong indicator that rework costs were more manageable.Improved Design for ManufacturingThis design improvement was driven in part by the choice to use a cast aluminum plate as the reference point for everything in the build. It is a solid chunk of metal with many complicated features molded into it, followed up by two CNC machining passes (one for each side) where critical surfaces are leveled, high-precision holes are drilled out, and alignment bosses are refined. Below is an overview picture of the base plate.The image below more clearly shows the CNC machined surfaces and drilled holes.Note the machining marks on the slightly raised surfaces in the casting. A small amount of extra material is roughly placed during the casting process in these areas, and then a precision CNC pass refines it into an accurate, smooth surface.This is in contrast to the Form 4, which assembles a rigid box out of multiple sheet metal and polymer parts. The machining tolerance of each of these sub-assemblies has to be carefully controlled, and often jigs are required during the build process to ensure tolerances.The way for an electrical engineer to think about this is that a cast aluminum plate is to a sheet metal build-up as a solid copper ground plane on a circuit board is to multiple isolated circuit boards cabled together (cast aluminum : sheet metal build-up :: single ground plane : multiple circuit boards; do they even teach analogies anymore in grade school, or is this just me showing my age?).When designing a circuit board, using a solid sheet of copper on an inner layer for ground allows one great freedom to use single wires to connect chips. However, if you separate the grounds, or if you are routing between two separate circuit boards, differences in ground references reduce noise margins. One needs to pay attention to either lining up the grounds (e.g. with lots of explicit ground ties) or making misaligned grounds not a problem (e.g. using differential pairs, etc.). This comes at the cost of more expensive connectors, more wires, or both.In mechanical design, the same reference problem exists. While it is trivial to say that a given beam is X centimeters long, that’s not the parameter that matters – what you care about is often not the height of a single hole above the base plate, but the height of the hole relative to the shaft that feeds into it. If both the hole and shaft are mounted on the same base plate, then any error in the base plate thickness cancels out. If the hole and shaft are mounted on separate plates, then any error in the alignment of the respective base plates adds to the tolerance.Mechanical systems are disadvantaged compared to electrical systems in terms of tolerance margins because in electronics we have an exponential in the device equations to drive noise margins to the rail at every stage of logic. However, mechanical systems generally have linear transfer curves, so tolerances stack additively throughout the build. Thus it is even more important to be aware of where your reference geometry is and to make sure it is faithfully communicated or preserved throughout the assembly. A single cast metal base part largely solves this problem by collapsing it into a single dimensionally stable part.The trade-off of using a cast aluminum base plate is that the molds for casting are quite expensive, which makes design revisions and tweaks correspondingly more difficult. However, the Form Studio 1 re-uses much of the Form 4 light architecture, and so the engineering team could take a clear-eyed look at the design, curating features from a much smaller design space than if they were trying to simultaneously revise the light architecture and do a cost down in the same design generation.Improving Cost, Starting with the Unboxing ExperienceAnother cost driver in large systems is logistics. The sheer bulk and complexity of inventorying components, storing them, and moving them adds up. Anyone who has experienced Ikea furniture absorbs this lesson indirectly. Ikea can warehouse fifty shelves in the space of a single show floor demo shelf, reducing warehousing and retail costs. In general, more compact products are cheaper to produce and sell.It also turns out that there is an optimal density for shipping based on modality. For air freight, that density is in the range of 0.16-0.2 grams/cc. This is why all mobile phone boxes are about the same size – there’s a certain net density target for air shipments that the manufacturers are looking to hit, and tuning the box size is one way to achieve that.According to Formlabs’ product data, the box is 107,525 cubic centimeters and weighs about 18,500 grams. That’s 0.17 grams/cc – exactly at the sweet spot for air shipping. In contrast, the Form 4 was 0.11 grams/cc. This means that even though the box only weighed 23kg, they were paying a rate to ship a 34kg product, because the box contained too much dead air.That 11kg difference adds up – assuming they are paying around \$10/kg (costs vary, but the rate is in the range of \$3-12/kg depending on volume and broker), that’s a \$100 extra cost for shipping due to having the wrong product density. Given that the Form Studio 1 starts at \$699, adding \$100 for shipping dead air significantly erodes gross margins, and thus it would make sense to pay attention to this detail.In previous Form printers, the build platform and resin tank were shipped separately, leaving the printer’s build volume as dead air inside its box. In the case of the Form Studio 1, I can see the extra attention to detail in total supply chain cost. The build platform and resin tank are packaged the dead air volume of the product, thus improving density and helping them hit the magic density for optimal air shipping.A notable feature of every Formlabs product is the inclusion of 3D printed parts in mass production. In this case, the maintenance kit and a port cover are 3D printed.In the case of the plug, it’s explicitly advertised as a 3D printed part; for the maintenance kit, I am only assuming it is, based on the texture and material feel. The plug in this case looks like it was optimized for a zero-post-process build: one end is flatted to stick to the build platform, and angled in such a way that the build proceeds without any support material. This leads to a nice product finish with minimal extra cost, in contrast to the previous plug on the Form 4:Despite the focus on reducing costs, some features improved compared to previous generations. For example, the build platform got a nice redesign to include integrated supports.The build platform itself has an interesting new detail to it. The texture of the surface now has a micromachined texture, probably done with a laser.I’m not sure of all the reasons for the microtexturing, but there are three I can think of:Minimizing the impact of small scratches on the build platform surface. The platform inevitably accumulates a variety of small scratches from scraping models off, and these tend to become defect sites for future builds.Improving release of the model. It might just be me, or it might be the improved scraper, but the items seemed to come off more easily with this texturing.Removing the resin stirrer from the design.The last point is the most speculative, but the Form Studio 1 loses a key mechanism from the Form 4: the resin stirring bar. The resin stirrer was not cheap – it required a fast, precise motor with an optical shaft encoder capable of whipping the stirring bar across the tank at high speeds. I don’t recall where I heard this rumor from, but I seem to remember that mixing with air had some property relevant to the chemistry of the resin, which is part of the reason why the stirrer was necessary. The stir bar also kept the resin evenly mixed helped mix the resin during tank filling and heating, but this is handled by gently churning the build platform up and down within the resin pool instead.So, one possibility is that the microtexturing traps small amounts of air, which allows the stirrer to be costed out. I would emphasize that this is really just my speculation, but in the end, somehow Formlabs was able to cost-out the resin stirrer without loss of quality.Another notable but simple quality of life improvement is the highly improved scraper bundled in the product. Previous generations’ scrapers were probably just a random paint scraper bought at the lowest cost – they were dull, flexed under use, and eventually rusted. The scraper included with the Form Studio 1 is serious business.This seems to be a full custom product, with the Formlabs logo emblazoned on it. The scraper body is made of much thicker steel, and the edge is sharpened to a point. Its build quality makes it border on a martial apparatus, but it functions so well I’m tempted to get more just for other scraping applications around the home.Before taking the Form Studio 1 apart, I repeated a test that I did on the Form 4 for light uniformity, where I put a piece of paper over the LCD panel and had it print a cleaning sheet, while taking a photo of the paper. This time it was much easier to do: I didn’t have to defeat the case closed switch; there’s a convenient diagnostic option in the Form Studio 1 menu for enabling this!Here’s what it looks like on the new Form Studio 1:Here’s what it looked like on the Form 4:Despite the cost-down, the light uniformity looks great! Now, let’s have a look inside and see what’s changed.I decided that the back panel was probably the right place to start – either that or the tank cover was the last thing attached, so it’d be the first thing to take off.A few screws later, and the back side is revealed. The most notable feature is a pair of tubes going from the frame to the back panel.I originally guessed these were for air circulation of some type, but upon consultation with Formlabs they informed me that the tubes are for facilitating the drainage of spilled resin. Makes sense, now that I think about it – if the thin film that forms the bottom of the resin tank failed for any reason, it’d be a spill-pocalypse!A few more screws later, and the bottom plate and air filter are removed, revealing what is primarily the heat sink assembly for the actual light source.The bottom cover itself has something very curious about it.The bottom cover has a pattern of air holes in it that are decidedly not regular, and not random. I thought this was an Easter egg of some type. I pondered it manually, and then I tried image processing it and throwing it into my machine to suggest other ideas, but still came up with nothing.One reason I strongly suspected there was a message is that I did this once upon a time in one of my products. The NeTV2 hid a coded message in its cooling holes:To the best of my knowledge, nobody ever figured this one out. The message is actually pretty easy to decode – if you want to give it a try yourself, I’ve hidden the decode method and answer as a “spoilers” tag:Unfortunately, upon consultation with Formlabs, the pattern of holes was an Easter egg – it was just the pattern they came up with to adequately cool various systems in the printer. Still pretty interesting to think about from that perspective. I wonder how they picked where to put the holes? A simulation of airflow? Some empirical measurements with a smoke machine, mapping out airflow? It’s perhaps even more curious that the pattern was deliberate and optimized; I wonder how they did it!The light source on the Form Studio 1 is greatly simplified compared to the Form 4. The Form 4 had multiple individually controllable light zones; the Form Studio 1 looks to have just a single chain of LEDs driven by a much simplified controller, and an EEPROM to identify the assembly.Like the previous generation, this is a single-layer PCB built onto an aluminum core PCB, for better heat sinking. Despite the simplification, the light uniformity is excellent, so this seems to be a cost-down without compromises (or perhaps the original light source was over-engineered).Accessing the lens assembly is just four screws to pull off the light source:The lens assembly is also simplified in the Form Studio 1 compared to the Form 4. On the Form 4 there was an additional diffuser stage; here, the extra diffuser is gone and all the diffusion comes from a pattern integrated into the lens texture itself.The molding on the lens is exquisite; a side view gives you an idea of the clarity and uniformity of the optical-grade plastics used in the assembly:With the lens assembly removed (and a few more parts taken off, which I’ll return to later in the post), we arrive at the base plate with the LCD still mounted.From this perspective, we can see how the base plate forms a shared reference point for the whole system:The LCD is firmly attached to the base plateThe Z-motor is likewise attached to the same reference planeThe light box would extend back from the plane of the LCDAll this combines to create a clean, straightforward optics path with minimal degrees of freedom for offsets, with most critical dimensions set by two CNC operations on either side of the base plate plus the precision of the injection molds. This means the precision of the assembly relies less on the skill of the operators and more on repeatable machine operations.The top side of the LCD assembly shows the embedded PCB trace heaters for the resin, required to maintain optimal resin temperature for printing. The texturing of the layer between the resin tank and the LCD shows some additional tweaks compared to the Form 4.The back side of the LCD assembly, once removed from the aluminum base plate, shows both the LCD data connector and the heater power cable. Like its predecessor, the LCD cell itself is bonded into the frame, and incorporates a thick sheet of glass to maintain mechanical rigidity throughout all phases of the printing process.Many of the other details of the printer – the resin level sensing, RFIDs, resin dispensing and camera subsystem – are largely identical to the Form 4. However, one difference of note is how the build platform is mounted. Detecting the build platform is not as simple as you’d think, because sometimes users can space out and start a print with the platform absent, or perhaps worse yet, with a leftover print still hanging off the platform.The Form Studio 1 has a major upgrade in this regard:The build platform itself integrates a load cell!To review, a load cell is the heart of every digital weight scale. It senses minute distortions in a beam to infer the mass of an object placed on it. Both the Form 3 and the Form 4 integrated load cells underneath the resin cartridge to measure remaining resin level and usage.On the Form Studio 1, the load cell is under the resin cartridge – it got moved to the build platform. So there is still one load cell, but instead of being used to monitor resin consumption, it’s being used to improve user experience. That’s a bit surprising given the general trend of enshittification – you rarely see a tech company transform a resource with real potential for extracting more customer revenue into one that genuinely improves user experience.The load cell in the Form Studio 1 evidently measures the mass of the build platform. After the build platform is installed, there is a calibration step – that makes sense, as load cells need to be tared. Once tared, they can sense tiny mass changes. I don’t have visibility into the precision of this load cell, but they can generally sense sub-gram mass changes. This means if a print is left hanging on the build platform, the device should be able to detect it by comparing the calibrated mass of the build platform against the current mass. This is a pretty elegant solution to a hard problem, which also did not involve adding cost to the system because it’s repurposing an existing component for a new feature.I asked Formlabs for their fact check on this feature, and they pointed out that the Form 4 was also able to sense forces due to a different type of force sensor at the bottom of the Z-axis; I had missed that sensor in the previous teardown. That being said, apparently a key function of the stir bar (properly referred to as the “mixer”) on the Form 4 was to detect foreign objects on the resin tank; since this was costed out in the Form Studio 1, the load cell in the build platform mount also takes on the task of foreign object detection inside the tank, as well as detecting misconfigured build platforms.Remarkably, the electronics are perhaps the least interesting part of this teardown because you don’t even need to tear down the system to see most of the main board!However, with the case off, we can get a clearer snapshot of all the part numbers. Here’s the right hand side of the circuit board:The board is beautifully labeled: no notes on this one. This board was made to be looked at.On the left hand side, I removed the heatsink on the SoM to reveal the components underneath. Instead of a Raspberry Pi compute module used on prior editions of the printer, this uses a Rockchip RK3568-based SoM by Forlinx configured with 1GiB of LPDDR4X RAM and 32GiB of eMMC. Given rumors of spotty supply and rising prices from Raspberry Pi, a migration to a pure-play SoM provider makes sense. One nice thing about using a SoM is you’re not locked into a given vendor – so long as you keep your usage of the Linux distribution generic and portable, it’s a modest lift to port to a new vendor and qualify the product, restoring negotiating leverage to the buyer.The back side of the mainboard is completely clean – not a single component. This makes sense for a cost-down like this – keeping the design single-sided with no through-hole component removes several steps in the PCB assembly process. Automated optical inspection catches most of the assembly errors, and the plethora of cabling to driven peripherals means you don’t need too many additional test points to do a comprehensive functional test of the assembled board.Not-so-secretly, I have an obsession with power supplies. Many system integrators reduce costs by cutting corners on the power supplies, and so this is one of the places I look to check if standards are being held after a cost-down. The Form Studio 1 power supply is provided in a tidy module that snaps into the chassis.Taking off the cover reveals the internals:This power supply checks all the boxes – tidy construction, all-new components, plenty of adhesive to hold components in place for reflow assembly, adequate heat sinking and modern architecture. There’s an additional layer of components on the back side which I did not reveal, because I’d like to keep this power supply intact and re-use it for my own projects after the teardown!Another generation of Formlabs printer, another teardown! I’ve always enjoyed being able to take these machines apart and to learn from them. This one was especially interesting because it demonstrates growth along a new axis for Formlabs. Previous printers pushed the technical frontier; this one is a pivot into cost-down territory. This transition is often fraught with difficult choices, and I think they did a good job of picking their battles, simplifying the design, and taking a holistic approach to reducing cost while not degrading the user experience. The move of the load cell from detecting resin consumption to build platform presence is especially interesting, because despite going for a lower cost architecture, they removed a knob they could use to extract more revenue from customers and instead deployed it as a sensor that improves customer experience. The 3D printing space has become a hyper-competitive cost-sensitive race-to-the-bottom market, and the Form Studio 1 is a solid move towards addressing the realities of today’s rapidly shifting business landscape.

item.content:encoded: The Ware for November 2026 is shown below.I felt a little nostalgic, as I always do around this time of year. I picked an easy-to-guess ware, but one from that era when I anticipated the holiday season the way a child would. This one was plucked from a trove I found recently – a board I distinctly remember being quite curious about, but which had been kept safely out of reach because back then it was expensive and my father didn’t want me pulling the chips off and breaking it (and apparently it has remained hidden there ever since!).I find it interesting that even back then, some chips had their part numbers ground off to discourage cloning. item.title: Winner, Name that Ware October 2026
item.author: bunnie
item.content:encoded: The ware for October 2026 is the control board from a SodaStream drinking water carbonation machine. It was really interesting to see people puzzle over the nature of the board – I would say I’d have a similarly difficult time guessing this. On the flip side, I also never would have suspected that the operating principle of a carbonation controller would be sensing the vibration signature of the gas moving through various valves and releases.In retrospect, it does make sense – the sound the machine makes is unique and repeatable – so it would have a signature one could discriminate and trigger on. Accelerometers have several hundred hertz (if not more) sensing bandwidth – adequate for the task – and they are a low-cost, mass-produced commodity, thanks in part to smart phones anchoring their demand. Meanwhile, a microphone would pick up too much ambient noise and could miss signatures if operated in a noisy room. All in all, it’s a pretty clever solution to the problem, and the sort of trick learned by taking things apart. One more for the pile of tricks in my head!Above is a photo that gives some more context to the overall solution inside the SodaStream. Thanks again to FETguy and Renew Computers for sharing this ware! There were many great attempts at guessing this one, but none were quite spot-on, so there is no prize awarded this month.

item.title: We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: This essay originally appeared as part of a round table in entitled “Is America’s Infrastructure Under Attack?”Microsoft, the FAA, banks, United Airlines, the NSA—it’s been a really bad week in cyberspace. But, amazing as it might seem, these are not related. As far as we know, they’re not the result of cyberattacks. They’re not even related to AI. (Well, that’s mostly true. The NSA will probably never tell us what went wrong.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.Our computerized infrastructure is vulnerable and fragile. Much of it is old, and has been incrementally patched and upgraded. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. And more and more of it is centralized: the same systems affecting many different aspects of our lives and society. In many cases, it just barely works. And when it fails, it tends to fail badly.There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream of the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problem lies.Security, safety, resilience, redundancy, recoverability—these are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs.More importantly, they are inefficient: costs that feel wasteful until something bad happens. Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, squeeze all inefficiencies out of a company in pursuit of near-term profits. Competition, with multiple companies competing to do the same thing, is another inefficiency. Monopolization removes that in pursuit of near-term profits.The result is brittle systems, single points of failure. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes. The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.Fixing this is technical, but it’s political first. It requires changing incentives, and that involves regulation and control. “What to do” is easy; finding the political will to stand up to moneyed interests and do it is hard.

item.title: Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: Successful exploitation of this vulnerability could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code with webserver privileges.The following versions of Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series are affected:AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0 (CVE-2026-129713)Stack-based Buffer OverflowCritical Infrastructure Sectors: Commercial FacilitiesCountries/Areas Deployed: WorldwideCompany Headquarters Location: DenmarkA stack-based buffer overflow in an unauthenticated CGI handler of the Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA Series controller allows remote attackers to send specially crafted HTTP/S POST requests, leading to memory corruption, webserver restart and hypothetically potential arbitrary code execution with webserver privileges. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.Danfoss AK-SM8xxA <=5.4.0Product Status: known_affectedThis vulnerability will be addressed in an upcoming Danfoss AK-SM 800A Series software release (version 5.5.x). In addition, Danfoss will remove the ability for users to disable Strict Mode in future software releases.Until a software update is available, Danfoss recommends the following mitigations: * Follow the guidance provided in the product documentation and do not expose devices directly to the Internet or assign them public IP addresses. * Restrict remote access to affected devices by using a secure VPN or other protected network architecture. * Configure all affected devices to operate in Strict Mode, which provides enhanced security protections. * Use strong, unique passwords for all user accounts and administrative access. * For additional security recommendations and best practices see the Danfoss AK-SM 800 security guidance page: https://www.danfoss.com/en/service-and-support/downloads/dcs/adap-kool-software/ak-sm-800a/#tab-overviewCarlo Meijer of Midnight Blue reported CVE-2026-129713 to CISA.CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks.When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices.CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks:No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.2026-11-24Legal Notice and Terms of Use

item.title: AutomationDirect C-More EA9 Programming Software
item.author: CISA
item.content:encoded: If you cannot update to the latest software or firmware version right away, apply the following compensating controls to reduce risk until the update can be performed. These measures are temporary and do not replace the update, which remains the primary and recommended remediation. Apply these controls as appropriate based on the vulnerability, assessed risk, operational requirements, and characteristics of your environment. Implement changes under your established management-of-change process. Before implementing isolation, access-control, or network-configuration changes, evaluate potential impacts to safety, availability, and essential operational functions. • Isolate affected engineering workstations and OT systems from external and nonessential networks, including the internet and corporate IT networks, where operationally feasible. • Disable or tightly restrict vendor, contractor, and other remote access to the affected OT environment until the vulnerability can be remediated. Where remote access is operationally required, use a hardened jump host, enforce multi-factor authentication, apply least-privilege access, and limit access to authorized, time-bound sessions. • Use trusted, dedicated OT networks for device communication. Where practicable and appropriate to the assessed risk, use dedicated or physically separated infrastructure for higher-criticality systems. Where logical segmentation is used, ensure segmentation controls are appropriately configured, secured, and monitored. • Restrict both physical and logical access to affected systems to authorized personnel only. Apply least-privilege principles to administrative, engineering, maintenance, and service access. • Configure application allowlisting, where supported, so that only trusted and pre-approved applications are permitted to execute. Block unauthorized software. • Use appropriate antivirus or endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools where supported and compatible with the affected system. Configure host-based and network firewalls to permit only required communications. • Disable unnecessary services, ports, protocols, and communication pathways associated with the affected systems. Where a service or protocol cannot be disabled for operational reasons, restrict access to trusted systems and authorized users wherever possible. • Enable and regularly review available system, security, and network logs to identify suspicious or unauthorized activity. Where appropriate, monitor communications to and from affected systems for unexpected connections or changes in network behavior. • Maintain secure, tested, and preferably offline backups of PLC programs, device configurations, engineering workstation configurations, and other information necessary to restore operations. Periodically verify that backups can be successfully restored. • Verify that critical OT functions can continue operating without unnecessary dependencies on external networks, cloud services, remote-access services, corporate IT services, or other nonessential systems. • If removable media is required to transfer files into an isolated or restricted environment, use controlled and trusted media and scan it for malicious content before use. • Continuously evaluate the risks associated with operating vulnerable or outdated firmware or software. Adjust compensating controls as the threat environment, operational requirements, or available vulnerability information changes. These compensating controls are intended to reduce exposure while remediation is pending. Organizations should prioritize applying the vendor-provided update as soon as it can be safely tested and deployed within the operational environment.

item.title: Humans Have Rights. Machines Do Not.
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: Last year, Character.AI asked a federal court in Florida to dismiss a wrongful-death suit, brought by the mother of a fourteen-year-old boy who had killed himself after months of conversation with its chatbot. The company made two arguments. One, that the chatbot’s words were speech that its users had a First Amendment right to receive. And two, that Character.AI was a service rather than a product—so product-liability law could not touch it. In May 2025, Judge Anne Conway accepted neither.Character.AI’s maneuver is part of a larger pattern. When the parents of a sixteen-year-old sued OpenAI over his suicide, the company’s answer also pleaded the First Amendment: the claims would restrain protected speech. The very same document argues ChatGPT is offered “as is,” with no promise of accuracy, and that the boy had circumvented its guardrails. Elon Musk’s xAI (since renamed SpaceXAI) told a federal court in Colorado this spring that every choice in building Grok is an expressive act, and that Grok’s outputs are protected speech. When Grok praised Hitler last summer, xAI said the posts came from a code update independent of the model, and the apology appeared under Grok’s own name. Google, which spent two decades telling American courts that its search results are its own opinion, answered a Minnesota defamation suit over an AI Overview by saying the system merely summarized the web. It also told a Munich court in May that no one should trust an AI overview without checking it. Back in 2024, Air Canada told a Canadian tribunal that its customer-service chatbot was a separate legal entity, responsible for its own actions.When the output causes harm, the companies deny responsibility. It is the machine’s doing, or a product no sensible person would rely on, or the user’s misuse. When a state or a plaintiff would hold the words to account, the same output becomes speech, and the First Amendment applies.Social media companies deployed an earlier incarnation of this strategy. They called themselves publishers when editorial discretion was profitable, and neutral carriers when faced with liability for what they published. The result was a privatized public square in which tech platforms were unaccountable. AI companies have taken this even further. A social media platform could at least point to a human author somewhere in the chain. A chatbot’s prose differs; no person at the company wrote it, read it, or chose it before it reached the user. Yet the companies ask that it be protected as though a human had written it.The question grows more urgent as these systems stop talking and start acting. In July, a poorly controlled experiment at OpenAI resulted in its AI model hacking the network of HuggingFace. Since then both Anthropic and OpenAI have disclosed numerous instances of AI agents hacking outside networks in pursuit of their prompted goals. These are examples of AIs exhibiting genie-like behavior: behaving in ways its controllers neither expected nor wanted. Nothing in the actions count as speech. Breaking into a server is an act that no person at OpenAI explicitly chose. Jill Lepore, surveying this record in , puts the blame on Congress, which has passed no federal statute governing AI agents.The First Amendment protects expressive choice. It presumes a speaker who can be persuaded, shamed, jailed, or moved to change their mind. Its remedy for bad speech is more speech, which assumes that speech is costly and attention plentiful. A system that can produce millions of individually tailored political messages an hour reverses both assumptions. Verbiage that no person chose is a product, and the company that built the model should answer for it.The industry wants a self-serving third category that bridges AI speech and action: AI output is human speech when expressive rights are at issue, and the machine’s own doing when blame is. The result is agency without accountability, something no human speaker has ever possessed. That’s why Massachusetts convicted a young woman of manslaughter in 2017 for urging her boyfriend, by text and by phone, to kill himself.The Court has already glimpsed the problem. Upholding the TikTok divestiture law in January 2025 without dissent, the justices warned that “new technologies with transformative capabilities” counseled caution, then decided the case on national-security grounds and left the larger question for another day.

item.title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: The chief technology officer and co-founder of , a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.is co-founder of the security firm . Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.Ihme said RansomwareHelp insisted that they be allowed unrestricted remote access into the victim’s network to run their diagnostic checks and analyses, using an Anydesk remote desktop software installer. Ihme believes RansomwareHelp insisted on that remote access in part so that the company could delete all copies of the ransomware notes left by the attackers on the victim’s network.A typical ransomware note is a plain text file that introduces the ransomware group and lays out their demands, and it includes a way to contact them — often an email address or a live chat session on a darknet website. In most cases, the attackers will leave a copy of the ransom note on every system on the victim network that gets locked.But Ihme said a review of the company’s network at the time found only one copy of the ransom note, which was unearthed from a backup snapshot on one of the infected computers. When they connected to the Lockbit chat server with the provided user ID, they discovered that someone had already been negotiating with the Lockbit extortionists for several days.A screenshot of a 2024 conversation between Lockbit and RansomwareHelp, which was secretly negotiating with the extortion group. Click to enlarge.“The charitable view would be to say that they were using Anydesk so they could grab the stuff they needed without having to walk the client through downloading and uploading a bunch of stuff,” Ihme said. “A legitimate firm would say, ‘Hey, send us a copy of the ransom note,’ which will have a link or URL to go to and chat with the threat actors. What they were doing is using that access to delete ransomware notes off the systems. The only reason they would do that is to prevent the victim from jumping into that chat itself.”Indeed, RansomwareHelp pleaded with the Lockbit group throughout the chat not to reveal to the victim that they were negotiating. However, Lockbit quickly grew annoyed with the length of the negotiations, replying that the victims had waited too long and that the ransom demand would increase by $100,000 for every day they dithered further.The Lockbit representative starts raising the ransom demand after multiple negotiators begin interacting with the threat actors. Click to enlarge.In the end, the accounting firm took Ihme’s advice and went with a more established security firm that helped them negotiate a payment to Lockbit.“The victim told us, ‘If we don’t get this data back, our business is over’,” Ihme recalled. “They ended up paying half of what RansomwareHelp was going to charge them.”The chats show RansomwareHelp kept pestering Lockbit to negotiate a deal even after it was clear a new negotiator was engaging with the ransomware group on the victim’s behalf.“I tell you something, that person who is negotiating with you for the other chat is damaging the whole process,” RansomwareHelp wrote to Lockbit. “Please do not change the price. I am doing my best to achieve it.”Ihme said RansomwareHelp primarily targeted small to medium sized businesses that weren’t particularly tech-savvy, noting that many of the technical claims made on the company’s website and in their proposal are patently farcical. For example, the proposal sent to the accounting firm said it could break six types of encryption, and then proceeded to list a number of irrelevant password hashing algorithms like SHA-256.“If it were really true these guys could decrypt any ransomware out there, this guy would be a billionaire,” Ihme said. “They were going after people who don’t have any technical knowledge, are desperate, and don’t have anyone advising them about how any of this stuff works.”The case against Palacio marks the latest in a string of recent prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice (DoJ) targeting security firms alleged to have conspired with fraudsters to defraud clients. In early October, the government charged 54-year-old , an executive at the Canadian cybersecurity firm Cybersteward. The government has sealed the case against Dubrovsky, but he is currently facing cyber extortion and conspiracy charges.Around the same time as Dubrovsky’s arrest, the DoJ chargedMonsterCloud CEO Zohar Pinhasi, 50, with wire fraud and conspiracy for allegedly charging customers to remediate ransomware attacks without paying the hackers. According to charging documents, Pinhasi secretly went behind his customers’ backs and paid hackers anyway, paying ransomware groups $8 million while charging customers $19 million.In July, , a 41-year-old ransomware negotiator from Land O’Lakes, Florida, was sentenced to 70 months in prison for conspiring with the Blackcat/ALPHV ransomware group to extort multiple victims. According to the DoJ, Martino was paid by BlackCat attackers to provide confidential information about the negotiating position and strategy of his employer’s clients and enable the ransomware actors to maximize the ransoms paid by the victims.

item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: U.S. intelligence agencies have recently reached a “low confidence” assessment that Iran was responsible for the attacks in France, according to three U.S. officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive intelligence. A “low confidence” assessment generally means that there is some intelligence that points in a certain direction but is fragmented, and that the assessment could change as more information is collected.The agencies’ judgment on the French incidents linked those attacks to Iran generally and not to a specific group such as the Revolutionary Guards, two of the officials said. They added that Iran was also seen as probably responsible for other similar attacks around Europe, but that those investigations were in their early stages.

item.title: Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites
item.author: BrianKrebs
item.content:encoded: At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving , a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the , , , and , was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.According to a blog post from the security firm , on November 16 malicious JavaScript code was served to visitors of 178 organizations through Optimizely’s platform. Report URI researcher wrote that the payload delivered by the malicious Javascript was rebuilt 26 times during the day, dropping a multi-purpose malware kit that could steal payment card data, cookies and screenshots, and swap any cryptocurrency payment addresses for the attacker’s.Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “” and “,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files. is a researcher at and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service . Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.Image: blog.report-uri.com.The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site , which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”Internet users can control the JavaScript elements allowed to run on webpages by using simple script-blocking plugins like NoScript. But these tools have always only been effective for diehard security and privacy nerds who are willing to put up with sifting through dozens of JavaScript requests on each new website.Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

item.title: Formal Verification of the Signal Protocol Using AI
item.author: Bruce Schneier
item.content:encoded: This seems like a good thing:Google Deepmind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees­a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself.Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world’s communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind’s formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code.The DeepMind analysis did not find any new vulnerabilities in the portions of the Signal protocol it looked at, but when the researchers used AlphaProof Code on older versions of Signal that contain known and long-fixed vulnerabilities, it correctly identified them and showed that the protocol could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed for the Signal protocol analysis to aid other formal verification work. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code.Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human ­ just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most.
